steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper on hierarchical optimization-based whole-body control for legged robots doing loco-manipulation of heavy objects: background, why it is hard, how existing planning/control frameworks handle it, and what our framework does.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Legged robots have been getting more and more attention because they could perform versatile locomotion tasks across challenging terrains. To make them more practically useful, researchers have looked at two approaches for loco-manipulation: using the robot's body or its existing limbs, and integrating articulated robotic arms into legged platforms so they can do loco-manipulation tasks. Combining locomotion and manipulation capabilities opens up exciting opportunities for legged robots in many real-world applications, from search and rescue missions to industrial automation.

However, getting loco-manipulation to work on legged robots is a formidable challenge. Legged robots are not like traditional wheeled or tracked robots, and they have unique dynamics and control intricacies when they manipulate objects. Manipulation forces and interactions with objects can introduce large disturbances that disrupt the stability and locomotion of the robot.

In recent years learning-based methods for loco-manipulation problems have received more attention, but classic control frameworks are still prevalent. Loco-manipulation means coordinating manipulation actions with the robot's environment and with locomotion. This usually involves two core components. One is a manipulation planner, which often computes plans offline, and the other is a locomotion tracking controller, which generates torque commands to track the high-level references set by the planner. The tracking problem is usually handled with various optimization frameworks that include the important system constraints. The planning module, on the other hand, tries to balance physical accuracy and computational complexity, and it often relies on simplified models of the problem. There are exceptions where the full system dynamics are used. But there is a common limitation: most of these formulations do not allow real-time solutions, so they are not suitable for fast online replanning.

- Unified nonlinear loco-manipulation framework in two recent works
  - nonlinear MPC planner: real-time trajectories for CoM, limbs, forces; whole-body controller tracks them
  - second work: offline planner for sequence of locomotion/manipulation actions, predefined library of interactions, user-defined tasks + environment model
  - nonlinear MPC: more detailed models/constraints, but significant computational power
- Our framework: legged agile loco-manipulation with whole-body coordination
  - MPC + pose optimization, coordinates locomotion and manipulation (Fig. 1)
  - nonlinear problem decomposed into elementary components interacting hierarchically
  - online pose optimization -> full coordination; complex tasks with custom-made 1-DOF arm
- Organization: II architecture; III, IV, V components; VI simulation and hardware results

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Legged robots have been getting more and more attention because they could perform versatile locomotion tasks across challenging terrains. To make them more practically useful, researchers have looked at two approaches for loco-manipulation: using the robot's body or its existing limbs, and integrating articulated robotic arms into legged platforms so they can do loco-manipulation tasks. Combining locomotion and manipulation capabilities opens up exciting opportunities for legged robots in many real-world applications, from search and rescue missions to industrial automation.

However, getting loco-manipulation to work on legged robots is a formidable challenge. Legged robots are not like traditional wheeled or tracked robots, and they have unique dynamics and control intricacies when they manipulate objects. Manipulation forces and interactions with objects can introduce large disturbances that disrupt the stability and locomotion of the robot.

In recent years learning-based methods for loco-manipulation problems have received more attention, but classic control frameworks are still prevalent. Loco-manipulation means coordinating manipulation actions with the robot's environment and with locomotion. This usually involves two core components. One is a manipulation planner, which often computes plans offline, and the other is a locomotion tracking controller, which generates torque commands to track the high-level references set by the planner. The tracking problem is usually handled with various optimization frameworks that include the important system constraints. The planning module, on the other hand, tries to balance physical accuracy and computational complexity, and it often relies on simplified models of the problem. There are exceptions where the full system dynamics are used. But there is a common limitation: most of these formulations do not allow real-time solutions, so they are not suitable for fast online replanning.

Recent studies have adopted a unified nonlinear loco-manipulation framework, for example one study and a later one. These works use a nonlinear Model Predictive Control planner that can compute real-time trajectories for the Center of Mass (CoM), the limbs, and the forces. Then a whole-body controller tracks these reference trajectories. In the second of these works, the authors introduce an offline planner that computes a sequence of locomotion and manipulation actions. It is guided by a predefined library of interactions, and this helps complete user-defined tasks that incorporate the environment model. However, nonlinear MPC has the advantage of considering more detailed predictive models or constraints, but it usually needs a lot of computational power because the nonlinear optimization problem is complex.

In this paper we present a novel framework for legged agile loco-manipulation that uses whole-body coordination to deal with the complexities of the task. Our approach combines elements of Model Predictive Control (MPC) and pose optimization to make a control strategy that coordinates locomotion and manipulation, as shown in Fig. 1. We designed a control structure that can execute loco-manipulation tasks by decomposing the nonlinear problem into elementary components that interact hierarchically. Using online pose optimization gives full coordination between manipulation and locomotion, and this is shown by the complex tasks we can do with the custom-made 1-DOF robot arm that we introduce in this paper.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the proposed control architecture and briefly explains the hierarchical interactions between the components. Sections III, IV, V explain each of these components in detail. Then Section VI shows the results of the simulation and hardware experiments.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Legged robots have garnered increasing attention for their potential to perform versatile locomotion tasks across challenging terrains [1,2,3,4,5]. To make them more practically applicable, researchers have explored two approaches to loco-manipulation: utilizing the robot's body or existing limbs [6,7,8], and integrating articulated robotic arms into legged platforms so that they can execute loco-manipulation tasks [9,10,11,12]. Combining locomotion and manipulation capabilities opens up exciting opportunities for legged robots in various real-world applications, from search and rescue missions to industrial automation [13,14,15,16].

However, achieving successful loco-manipulation with legged robots is a formidable challenge. Unlike traditional wheeled or tracked robots [17,18,19], legged robots face unique dynamics and control intricacies when manipulating objects. Manipulation forces and object interactions can introduce substantial disturbances that disrupt the robot's stability and locomotion [20,21].

Although learning-based methods for loco-manipulation problems have received increased attention in recent years [22,23,24], classic control frameworks remain prevalent. Loco-manipulation requires coordinating manipulation actions with the robot's environment and locomotion. This typically involves two core components: a manipulation planner, which often computes plans offline, and a locomotion tracking controller that generates torque commands to track the high-level references set by the planner [25,26,27,28]. The tracking problem is typically tackled with various optimization frameworks that accommodate the crucial system constraints [29,30]. The planning module, in contrast, tries to strike a balance between physical accuracy and computational complexity, and frequently relies on simplified models of the problem [31,32]. There are, nevertheless, exceptions where the full system dynamics are employed [33,34]. Yet a common limitation remains: most of these formulations do not allow real-time solutions, which makes them unsuitable for rapid online replanning.

Recent studies, such as [35] and [36], have adopted a unified non-linear loco-manipulation framework. These works use a nonlinear Model Predictive Control planner capable of computing real-time trajectories for the Center of Mass (CoM), limbs, and forces, and a whole-body controller then tracks these reference trajectories. In [36], the authors introduce an offline planner that computes a sequence of locomotion and manipulation actions. Guided by a predefined library of interactions, this process helps complete user-defined tasks that incorporate the environment model. It is important to note, however, that while nonlinear MPC has the advantage of considering more detailed predictive models or constraints, it typically requires significant computational power because of the complexity of the nonlinear optimization problem.

This paper presents a novel framework for legged agile loco-manipulation that leverages whole-body coordination to tackle the inherent complexities of the task. Our approach integrates elements from Model Predictive Control (MPC) and pose optimization into a control strategy that coordinates locomotion and manipulation, as illustrated in Fig. 1. We have devised a control structure that can execute loco-manipulation tasks by decomposing the nonlinear problem into elementary components that interact hierarchically. Online pose optimization enables full coordination between manipulation and locomotion, as demonstrated by the complex tasks we can perform with the custom-made 1-DOF robot arm introduced in this paper.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the proposed control architecture, briefly explaining the hierarchical interactions between the components. Sections III, IV, V explain each of these components in detail. Section VI then shows the results of simulation and hardware experiments.
